nameStory: The Stilt Sandpiper gets its name from its remarkably long, thin legs that look like walking sticks or stilts! The scientific name backs this up too - 'himantopus' comes from ancient Greek meaning 'strap foot' or 'thong foot,' referring to those distinctive stilt-like legs. When you see one wading in deeper water than other sandpipers, you'll understand why early bird watchers thought of stilts.
description: The Stilt Sandpiper is a medium-sized shorebird that stands out from the sandpiper crowd with its unusually long legs and slightly curved bill. About robin-sized, it has a sleek build perfect for wading in deeper water than most of its cousins. In breeding plumage, it sports rusty-red patches on the face and underparts with bold barring, while in fall and winter it appears more gray-brown and plain. This elegant wader is an uncommon but regular visitor to New England during migration.

idTips.label: Long yellowish legs
idTips.description: The legs are noticeably longer than other similar-sized sandpipers and have a distinctive yellowish or greenish-yellow color that stands out against muddy backgrounds

idTips.label: Slightly drooped bill
idTips.description: The bill has a subtle downward curve at the tip, longer and thicker than a Least Sandpiper's needle-like bill but not as curved as a Dunlin's

idTips.label: Feeding behavior
idTips.description: Often feeds by probing deeply into mud with a rapid, sewing machine-like motion, and will wade belly-deep in water where other sandpipers fear to go

idTips.label: White rump patch
idTips.description: In flight, shows a bright white patch above the tail that contrasts sharply with the darker back feathers

idTips.label: Breeding plumage face pattern
idTips.description: In spring and early summer, develops distinctive rusty-red ear patches and cheeks with a white stripe over the eye, creating a striking face pattern

habitat: Look for Stilt Sandpipers at shallow freshwater and brackish wetlands, including pond edges, flooded fields, sewage treatment ponds, and salt marsh pools. They prefer muddy or sandy-bottomed areas where they can probe deeply for food, often in slightly deeper water than other sandpipers use. Coastal salt ponds and inland reservoirs with exposed mudflats are particularly good spots during migration.

seasonality.spring: Uncommon migrant from late April through May, often showing partial breeding plumage with rusty face markings. Peak numbers usually occur in mid to late May.
seasonality.summer: Very rare in New England during summer months, as most birds continue north to Arctic breeding grounds. Any summer sightings are likely late spring migrants or early fall returnees.
seasonality.fall: More common during fall migration from July through September, appearing in plain gray-brown plumage. Adults arrive first in July, followed by juveniles in August and September.
seasonality.winter: Does not overwinter in New England, continuing south to tropical wintering grounds in South America by October.

funFact: Stilt Sandpipers are marathon migrants that can fly non-stop for over 2,000 miles from their Arctic breeding grounds to South America, sometimes crossing the entire Atlantic Ocean in a single flight - a journey that takes them 40+ hours without rest!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Dunlin, but Stilt Sandpipers have much longer, more colorful legs and a less curved bill. Remember: 'Stilt = long stilts (legs)' while Dunlin have shorter, darker legs and hunch closer to the ground when feeding.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a sandpiper, Stilt Sandpipers often behave more like their yellowlegs cousins, wading in deeper water and picking food from the surface rather than just probing in sand. This intermediate behavior reflects their unique ecological niche among shorebirds.
compareHints: Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, the Stilt Sandpiper is the tallest and longest-legged, easily distinguished from the tiny 'peeps' like Least and Semipalmated Sandpipers. Compared to the medium-sized Dunlin, Stilt Sandpipers stand taller, have straighter bills, and show more white in the rump during flight. Unlike the chunky Red Knot, Stilt Sandpipers maintain a sleek, elegant profile.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the Calidris sandpipers, sanderlings are notably stockier with a thicker bill than the needle-billed Least Sandpiper or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Within the Calidris genus, Semipalmated Sandpipers are most similar to Western Sandpipers but have blunter, shorter bills and less rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among its Calidris cousins, the Least Sandpiper's yellow-green legs immediately set it apart from the black-legged Semipalmated and Sanderling.

Among the Calidris sandpipers, dunlin are larger than the "peeps" (semipalmated, least, and white-rumped sandpipers) but smaller than red knot, with that diagnostic curved bill that none of the others possess.
Among the many Calidris sandpipers, Purple Sandpiper is unique for its consistently dark plumage and exclusive rocky habitat preference.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, White-rumped is most similar to Baird's Sandpiper, but Baird's lacks the white rump and has a more buff-colored breast.

Among the Calidris sandpipers in New England, pectoral sandpipers are distinguished by their larger size and that signature sharp breast line - dunlin have curved bills and different streaking, while the various 'peeps' (least, semipalmated) are much smaller.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Red Knot is the second-largest and most robust, much chunkier than Sanderling or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among the small Calidris sandpipers, Baird's stands out with its notably long wing projection past the tail - much longer than Semipalmated or Least Sandpipers.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, Buff-breasted is unique for its solid peachy-tan underparts and preference for grassy areas over mudflats.

Among New England's small sandpipers, Western Sandpipers are most easily confused with Semipalmated Sandpipers, but Westerns have longer, more drooped bill tips and often show more rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among Calidris sandpipers, Ruffs are unique in their extreme sexual size difference - much more pronounced than in Dunlin or Pectoral Sandpipers.
Among its Calidris sandpiper relatives, the Curlew Sandpiper's curved bill immediately sets it apart from straight-billed species like Sanderling and Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among its Calidris relatives in New England, Little Stint is smaller than Least Sandpiper (already our tiniest regular sandpiper) and much smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Compared to other small Calidris sandpipers in New England, Red-necked Stint is smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper and has darker legs than Least Sandpiper.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Sharp-tailed is most similar to Pectoral Sandpiper in size and habitat preferences, but lacks the Pectoral's sharply cut breast band.
Among Calidris sandpipers, the Surfbird is uniquely stocky and rock-adapted, unlike its beach and mudflat-loving relatives.
